title: The steep throw and the flat throw
hook: Same arm, same speed: one ball at 30 degrees, one at 60. Which lands farther?

knows: that thrown things fall back down
doesNotKnow: splitting a velocity into horizontal and vertical parts
the range formula R = v^2 sin(2 theta) / g

misconception: A steeper throw goes higher and therefore farther (or a flatter throw goes farther because it heads toward the target); each angle has its own unique distance.
objective: The learner can explain that, ignoring air drag and launching from the ground, angles that add to 90 degrees (30 and 60, 20 and 70) land at the same spot: the steep throw stays up longer but drifts sideways slowly, the flat throw moves sideways fast but lands soon. 45 degrees, the balance point, goes farthest.

claims.text: Ignoring air resistance, a projectile launched from ground level at speed v and angle theta lands at distance R = v^2 sin(2 theta) / g.
claims.source: Flight time 2 v sin(theta) / g times horizontal speed v cos(theta), with sin(2 theta) = 2 sin(theta) cos(theta). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 4 (Projectile Motion).

claims.text: Angles that add up to 90 degrees give the same range, because sin(2 theta) = sin(180 degrees - 2 theta).
claims.source: From c1 and the identity sin(x) = sin(180 deg - x). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 4.

claims.text: At 20 m/s with g = 9.81 m/s^2, a 30 or 60 degree launch lands about 35.3 m away and a 45 degree launch about 40.8 m away.
At 20 m/s, a 60 degree throw stays in the air about 3.5 s and peaks about 15.3 m high; a 30 degree throw stays up about 2.0 s and peaks about 5.1 m high.
claims.source: Flight time 2 v sin(theta) / g: 2 x 20 x 0.866 / 9.81 = 3.53 s, 2 x 20 x 0.5 / 9.81 = 2.04 s. Peak v^2 sin^2(theta) / (2 g): 15.29 m and 5.10 m.

claims.text: Ignoring air resistance and launching from the ground, 45 degrees gives the longest range.
claims.source: sin(2 theta) is largest (= 1) at 2 theta = 90 deg. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 4.

claims.text: With real air drag the two complementary throws no longer land together; the steep, long-flight throw loses more metres, so the flatter throw lands farther.
claims.source: Drag acts throughout the flight, so the longer flight loses more range, and the optimum angle drops below 45 deg. Fact-check 2026-10-12 numeric integration (linear and quadratic drag, pairs 20/70, 30/60, 40/50): the flatter throw lands farther in all 21 cases. Background: Taylor, Classical Mechanics (2005), ch. 2 (projectiles with linear and quadratic air resistance); section pin removed in v2 because 'sec. 2.4-2.5' looked mis-pinned.

claims.text: At 20 m/s, 20 and 70 degree throws both land 26.2 m away, and 40 and 50 degree throws both land 40.2 m away.
At 20 m/s the 60 degree ball moves sideways at 10 m/s and the 30 degree ball at about 17.3 m/s, so the steep ball drifts sideways more slowly.
claims.source: Horizontal speed v cos(theta): 20 cos 60 = 10; 20 cos 30 = 17.32.

claims.text: Ignoring air resistance, a ball thrown at 25 degrees and one at 65 degrees at the same speed land at the same spot.
claims.source: Recall question. 25 + 65 = 90, so c2 applies: sin(50 deg) = sin(130 deg).

claims.text: Ignoring air resistance, a ball thrown at 20 m/s and 25 degrees from the ground lands about 31.2 m away.
claims.source: c1: 400 sin(50 deg) / 9.81 = 31.23 m. Recall question (v2), matched to the lesson's 20 m/s after fact-check 2026-10-12 fix 4.

recall.question: Ignoring air resistance, a ball thrown at 20 m/s and 25 degrees lands 31.2 m away. At the same speed, which other angle lands at the same spot?
recall.why: Angles that add to 90 degrees share a landing point: the steep throw stays up longer but moves sideways more slowly.
